en: Her joints gave way as she sobbed;
She carried Chyiyrdy on her back,
Semetey was in her arms;
Bereft of any recourse, she cried out.
Her soles were pounded by stones,
Her temples scorched by the sun.
She found no cold water for her thirst,
No poison to end her life,
Nor, to take shelter in the shade,
A cooler place;
To die without further exhaustion,
She found no ready grave.
Dust covered and filled her mouth.
From a spring crossing her path, from running water,
Kanykei yearned for a single swallow.
Parted from her falcon,
Your bereft widow could not stand,
Reduced to such wretchedness.
Her gray-maned uncle Bakai—
She yearned for even one sight of him.
All her ribs and bones
Seemed to crack, collapse and come apart.
The dark blood flowing from her calves
Poured down into her boots.
The lady screamed in misery;
To reach her father Temir Khan
Your sister-in-law yearned terribly.
She had grown utterly exhausted.
When your mother cried “Oh!” blood came from her mouth.
Thirsty and hungry alike,
Your mother Kanykei lost her strength.
In mortal anguish she took as her support
Her one child Semetey;
Hungry, truly suffering hell,
Her thoughts scattered far and wide.
Clasping him with all her life,
Kanykei took as her support
The child left by the valiant warrior.
“Such is this wretched world,” she thought.
The noble woman Kanykei
Troubled her heart still more.
Following the trail, Bakai saw
The child she was carrying.
The horse Bakai led was Taitoru;
On Bakai's right was Akborchuk.
With a letter written for Bukhara,
Weeping and sobbing, for his orphan,
With two swift horses,
He had come searching.
Your father Bakai brought good fortune;
His lofty support was like a countless army.
When he saw Kanykei's figure,
He groaned with grief:
“Alas, leopard Manas, do not die!
Alas for this world!
When the khan dies, all have died;
Women and children crying out,
May you never wander in this way!
If it has happened so to her,
To whom might it not happen?
Such humiliation,
From now on, one God,
Do not grant your servant!” he said.
“God, do not take the lion!
Such humiliation
Do not impose upon your servant again!
Descendants of noble lords,
May you never be left wandering in the wilderness like this!
God, do not take the khan!
The only child of the prince,
Fleeing in fear to Bukhara,
May you never wander stripped of your dignity!
May no widow be left behind!
Bakai in his old age—
Do not lift him up and plunge him into misery!
Setting out toward Temir Khan,
Were you, fierce woman, meant to wander?
Roaming in search, unable to find you,
Was I, Bakai, meant to stare helplessly?
Walking on foot without boots,
Were you, my child, meant to sob?
Neither dying nor vanishing in the wilderness,
Was I, Bakai, meant to roar in grief?
When your royal lord died,
My child, fierce Kanykei,
Were you meant to flee in your stockings?
Parted from my orphan,
Still going about without sinking into the earth,
Was I, peerless Bakai, meant for this?
When my king Manas was alive,
Did I eat a raven's eye?
Unable to find his only child,
Alas, King Bakai—
Did you say he should be left to perish?”
Then your uncle Bakai, bearer of good fortune,
Caught up behind the fugitive.
Across Jorgonun-Bel they had driven
The sorrow-stricken, fierce woman;
They had driven her from broad Talas,
Across the pass of Kuyuk;
The orphan, still so tiny,
They had driven from broad Talas.
Bakai could not remain still for grief;
He had taken a letter written for Bukhara,
And for the sorrowful ones to ride,
To attain their wish,
He had brought two swift horses.
For their provisions, King Bakai
Had brought milk poured into a leather flask.
“To the orphan left by the gray-maned hero
They will do much violence,” he thought.
“God will strike those dogs down,” he said.
Taking two riding horses,
King Bakai came lamenting.
“My soft little gray-and-white falcon,” he said;
King Bakai came weeping.
“The morning star left by boundless Manas,” he said.
Your poor uncle Bakai's
Beard had grown thin;
The bloody tears flowing from his eyes
Poured down past his collarbone.
“O Kanykei, my foal,
You are ill-willed!
Not keeping your promise at all,
Your uncle Bakai in his old age—
You plunge him into hell like this!
O Kanykei, my foal,
Fleeing and traveling without stopping,
Have you eaten young sheep's meat?
Your mountain-like uncle, King Bakai—
Did you wish him to suffer your torment?
The gray winged steed ridden to Altai—
Did you wish it to grow thin?
Your uncle, finding no recourse,
Weeping much in a lonely place—
Did you wish him to become wretched?”
Then your uncle Bakai,
Lashing his whip to left and right,
Reached her and looked.
Kanykei had become wretched;
Her whole heart
Was aching then.
When he looked, her back
Was cut into strips like saddle-thongs.
Then your sister-in-law Kanykei's
Misery became plain.
That noble woman Kanykei—
Her whole back was raw with sores.
No strength remained; her power was gone.
With every stride of her poor feet,
Blood ran a saddle-thong's length.
“If this has happened to her,
To whom might it not happen?” he thought.
Then King Bakai's strength deserted him.
As the fierce woman fled without rest,
Her entire soles had grown raw.
Twelve bones, a thousand veins—
Alas, not one was free of pain.
“Let them ache; I shall die,” she thought.
“Allah's imposed command
Is this; I shall face it,” she thought.
“While I remain alive and not dead,
The orphan in my hands—
How can I give him to the enemy?” she thought.
Striding without stopping,
The precious woman Kanykei
Had fled with all her might.
To rest her life in any place,
She had not lain down, but fled.
O world, may you never prosper!
On the face of the earth, your widow
Had found no room, and fled.
Merciless torment
My precious child Kanykei
Had endured as she fled.
Ninety-year-old Chyiyrdy,
Taking her mother as her Mecca,
Upon her back Kanykei
Had borne her in flight.
When mighty Bakai reached her,
In some places Kanykei
Kept stubbornly pacing on.
The blood flowing from her calves
Streamed along the road.
With every movement she strode forward.
That swaddled Semetey,
“The little one left by my companion,” she said,
In the fold of her overskirt
The valiant woman Kanykei
Had fastened him securely for safekeeping.
To rest her life in any place,
The noble woman Kanykei
Had not lain down, but fled.
Two people could scarcely fit upon one person
As she fled.
Her ribs stood out;
My noble child Kanykei
Had grown thin.
My magnanimous lord, remain alive!
My precious child Kanykei
Had become wretched like this!
The famed gray-maned hero had died;
The fierce woman had suffered the hardship.
Your precious gray-maned hero had died;
Your fierce woman had suffered the torment.
Her soles had been pounded in the wilderness;
The whole of her forehead
Was scorched by the hot sun.
That warrior-built Kanykei,
Unable to endure it, grew frantic.
“The orphan left by my true one,” she said.
Kanykei could not endure it;
She met with real sickness.
Her dear, currant-black eyes—
Their lids were dusty and covered with dirt.
The valiant woman Kanykei
Had walked five days' journey in one stretch.
Her boots worn out, in stockings,
The poor little life still would not die.
Her overshoes worn out, in stockings,
The poor little life was grieving then.
When King Bakai reached her,
The peerless woman Kanykei's
Shoulder blades were raw with sores.
Not only humans, for the fierce woman
Even beasts felt pity.
Such was this fleeting world;
Now her widowhood was plain.
Her two moving feet
Were cut and torn to shreds.
Enduring grievous torment,
She had fled, twisting in anguish.
Had Bakai not come then,
Had your uncle not seen his widow,
Her dear hair, thick as a saddle-girth,
Was about to be braided.
That day, exhausted, Kanykei
Was about to die.
The strange road to the Last Judgment,
With calamity pressing upon her head,
She was about to see.
When your gray-maned Bakai arrived,
His orphan left by Manas,
When he took the child in his arms,
Allah's sun in the sky grew clouded.
Smelling the orphan's cheek,
Upon the hero Bakai's head
Sixty worries came at once.
“O Kanykei, my foal,
Today you have troubled my thoughts.
Journeying on a distant road,
You have carried away
My child left by my lord Manas.
My child, you have torn my heart,
O Kanykei, my foal,
You have burned my iron fortress.
